Ilakkiya, a staff engineer on our Platform team, reviewed my Skeinrouter design and wanted the main topic keyed by carrier ID, so rate limiting would fall out for free. I wanted shipment ID, because our top three carriers produce 38% of all events, so carrier keys meant a few very hot partitions. We went back and forth in doc comments for a week and got nowhere.

So I'd pick the service whose domain that data actually belongs to, make it the sole writer, and have the other one call an API or drop an event that the owner consumes. question: What's the worst production incident you've had to deal with? Walk me through it.
fallback_reason: direct DeepSeek for comparability: the baselines this run is compared with (er-dev-m1, er-dev-m1r) used direct DeepSeek; AgentRouter is available in this build and was not used
raw_answer:
The worst one was in November 2024, on Skeinrouter, the tracking pipeline I led at Quillhaven. We were in the fourth week of a per-carrier rollout, 720 carriers live, and a routine rolling restart of the 16 projector pods kicked off a rebalance storm. The group was still on eager rebalancing, so every pod restart stopped the whole group, and once the database was absorbing the backlog a batch could run past the 30-second max.poll.interval.ms, members got evicted for being slow, and each eviction triggered another rebalance.

I took incident command at 14:20, and we raised it to Sev-1 at 15:30 when lag peaked at 96 million events and the worst-hit shipments were 47 minutes behind. We paused the deploy, scaled the group down to 8 pods, and raised max.poll.interval.ms to 5 minutes, which stabilised it. Backlog drained by 17:45, so 3 hours 40 minutes total. No events were lost and nothing was rolled back, because the deduplication table kept the repeats out.

The follow-up mattered more. By 6 December we'd moved every consumer group to cooperative rebalancing with static membership, made rolling restarts go one pod at a time behind a lag gate of 200,000 events, and put a burn-rate alert on consumer lag.

[[GIST]] rebalance storm, 3h40m, fixed with cooperative rebalancing

fallback_reason: direct DeepSeek for comparability: the baselines this run is compared with (er-dev-m1, er-dev-m1r) used direct DeepSeek; AgentRouter is available in this build and was not used

Straight answer: the outbox part is a real match, the idempotency part is close but not the same shape.

On the outbox, Skeinrouter has exactly that pattern. The shipment-projector writes the state change and the outbox row in the same PostgreSQL transaction, and outbox-relay reads it with SKIP LOCKED and publishes. That's the JD's "outbox per service" almost word for word.

On idempotency, what I built is idempotent consumers, not idempotency keys on the write API. The dedup table is keyed on event ID and carrier ID, so replays and redeliveries become no-ops. The JD is asking for idempotency keys on every write endpoint, which is a client-supplied key on the request path, and I haven't built that.

So I'd say the outbox is a direct hit, and the idempotency is the same problem solved at the consumer side rather than the API side. I'd be honest about that gap rather than claim I've done both.

question: Have a look at TryConsume in the quota file. Is that safe when a lot of requests for the same tenant land together? And have you run into that sort of thing for real?
fallback_reason: direct DeepSeek for comparability: the baselines this run is compared with (er-dev-m1, er-dev-m1r) used direct DeepSeek; AgentRouter is available in this build and was not used
raw_answer:
No, it's not safe. TryConsume does a read under RLock, releases it, then writes under a separate Lock, so two goroutines for the same tenant can both read the same used value and both pass the limit check. It's a classic check-then-act race, and the fix is to do the read and the increment under one write lock, or use an atomic counter.

I've hit exactly this shape of bug before. On Skeinrouter I made every consumer idempotent with a deduplication table in PostgreSQL keyed on event ID and carrier ID, which cut duplicate status webhooks from 0.6% of deliveries to under 0.01%.

[[GIST]] check-then-act race, needs one lock

## Approach
Two pointers, one from each end, skipping anything that isn't a letter or digit and comparing lowercased characters. That gives linear time and constant extra space, which is what the sheet asks for. I'll keep the name `is_palindrome` exactly as written.

## Code
```python
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        while i < j and not s[i].isalnum():
            i += 1
        while i < j and not s[j].isalnum():
            j -= 1
        if s[i].lower() != s[j].lower():
            return False
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return True
```

## Complexity
Time O(n), each character is visited at most once by the two pointers. Space O(1), only the two indices, no copy of the string.

[[GIST]] two pointers, skip non-alphanumeric

question: notification system from the brief: can the sms vendor keep up at peak or do i need to buffer? give me the numbers
fallback_reason: direct DeepSeek for comparability: the baselines this run is compared with (er-dev-m1, er-dev-m1r) used direct DeepSeek; AgentRouter is available in this build and was not used
raw_answer:
SMS is 5% of 180 million a day, so about 9 million messages a day, which averages roughly 104 per second. Peak is 6 times average, so about 625 per second, and the vendor caps at 500 per second. So yes, at peak you exceed the vendor's limit and you need a buffer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    api["Send API"] -->|"enqueue"| queue["Notification Queue"]
    queue --> worker["Channel Worker"]
    worker -->|"SMS, rate limited"| sms["SMS Vendor 500/s"]
    worker -->|"push"| push["Push Provider 20k/s"]
    worker -->|"email"| email["Email Provider"]
    worker -->|"record attempt"| log[("Delivery Log")]
    worker -->|"failed, attempts left"| retry["Retry Queue with backoff"]
    retry --> worker
    worker -->|"attempts exhausted"| dlq["Dead-Letter Queue"]
```

The arithmetic: 180 million times 0.05 is 9 million SMS a day. Over 86,400 seconds that is about 104 per second average. Times 6 for the campaign burst gives about 625 per second, which is 125 per second over the vendor's 500. So the queue absorbs the burst and the worker drains it at a fixed 500 per second, which means a burst of that size clears in a bit over the burst window rather than being dropped. Push is nowhere near its 20,000 per second ceiling, so only SMS needs the throttle. The tradeoff is latency: transactional SMS still has to hit the 2 second p99, so those go on a priority path ahead of promotional traffic in the same queue.
